frameworks.governing_body: National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST)
frameworks.description: Voluntary framework providing guidelines for managing cyber risk using functions and categories
frameworks.name: NIST Cybersecurity Framework
weaknesses: Not a compliance standard; no audit/certification mechanism (unlike ISO 27001)
High-level language requires interpretation; orgs must decide implementation
Version 2.0 changes may confuse organizations still on 1.1
frameworks.when_required: Voluntary; requested by customers, investors. Mandatory for certain US federal contracts (EOs 14028, 14110)

top_level_functions.description: Establish org structure, policies, roles, responsibilities for cybersecurity
top_level_functions.name: GOVERN

top_level_functions.description: Establish safeguards to enable org ability to protect against cyber attacks
top_level_functions.name: PROTECT

top_level_functions.description: Develop capabilities to identify and understand cyber attacks
top_level_functions.name: DETECT

top_level_functions.description: Take actions to stop and mitigate impacts of detected cyber attacks
top_level_functions.name: RESPOND

top_level_functions.description: Restore normal operations after confirmed cyber attacks
top_level_functions.name: RECOVER

strengths: Widely recognized globally; applicable to all sectors and org sizes
Outcome-based (results-focused, not prescriptive), allowing flexibility
Integrates with other frameworks (ISO 27001, CIS Controls, ITIL)
New GOVERN function addresses board/C-suite responsibilities (2.0 update)
frameworks.primary_audience: All organizations, especially critical infrastructure; no compliance mandate

frameworks.description: International standard for establishing, implementing, maintaining ISMS. Audited and certified.
frameworks.name: ISO/IEC 27001
frameworks.when_required: Voluntary but demanded by large customers (banks, defense, healthcare). Competitive advantage in regulated sectors.
weaknesses: Certification is expensive and time-consuming (1-3 years for audit)
Compliance-heavy; some controls may not align with org context
Large control set (93) can be overwhelming for small orgs; scaled approach needed
strengths: Globally recognized certification; valued by enterprises and auditors
Prescriptive controls; clear implementation guidance
Integrates closely with risk management (ISO 31000)
Regular updates (2022 version current); evolving with threat landscape
frameworks.primary_audience: Organizations seeking information security management system (ISMS) certification

frameworks.structure: 5 Trust Service Principles (Principles), multiple controls per principle
frameworks.description: Audit standard evaluating controls over security, availability, processing integrity, confidentiality, privacy over operating period
frameworks.name: SOC 2 Type II
frameworks.when_required: Increasingly required by enterprise customers for B2B SaaS; de facto standard for US cloud vendors
weaknesses: Expensive (audits cost –+); time-intensive for small providers
Type I (point-in-time) less valuable than Type II; Type II requires 6+ months
Scope is customizable; 'lightweight' scope may not satisfy customers

top_level_principles.description: System protected from unauthorized access, disclosure, use
top_level_principles.name: Security

top_level_principles.description: System available as contracted; capacity and performance maintained
top_level_principles.name: Availability

top_level_principles.description: System processes, completes intended transactions completely, accurately
top_level_principles.name: Processing Integrity

top_level_principles.description: Information designated as confidential is protected from unauthorized disclosure
top_level_principles.name: Confidentiality

top_level_principles.description: Personal information collected, used, retained, disclosed per privacy notice
top_level_principles.name: Privacy

strengths: Highly valued by enterprise customers for cloud/SaaS vendors
Type II (operating effectiveness over period) provides assurance of sustained controls
Flexible scope; orgs choose which principles relevant to their service
Auditor attests to control design AND operating effectiveness
frameworks.primary_audience: Service providers (SaaS, cloud, hosting, MSP) assessed by independent auditors

frameworks.structure: 18 Controls organized by Implementation Groups (IG1, IG2, IG3)
frameworks.description: Prioritized, practical controls based on attacker tactics (MITRE ATT&CK mapped). Action-oriented.
frameworks.name: CIS Critical Security Controls

top_level_controls.description: Asset management, email/web protection, admin control, secure config (basic baseline)
top_level_controls.name: Safeguards

top_level_controls.description: Incident response, threat awareness, logging, testing (intermediate)
top_level_controls.name: Advanced

top_level_controls.description: Advanced threat hunting, extended detection, application security (advanced)
top_level_controls.name: Expert

frameworks.when_required: Recommended for critical infrastructure; increasingly adopted by gov and large enterprises. Not mandated but expected.
weaknesses: Less formal than ISO 27001; no audit/certification mechanism
18 controls are still a lot for small orgs; IG1 helps but still challenging
Threat-focused; may miss compliance-specific controls (audit, retention)
strengths: Practical, action-driven; not just policy language
Mapped to MITRE ATT&CK; shows how controls prevent specific techniques
Tiered approach (IG1/2/3) allows scaling by org maturity
Free available resources (benchmarks, tools) for implementation
frameworks.primary_audience: Defenders (IT, security teams) seeking practical, prioritized security actions

frameworks.governing_body: PCI Security Standards Council (Visa, Mastercard, American Express, Discover, JCB)
frameworks.description: Industry standard (not law) for protecting cardholder data. Enforced by card networks via fines/penalties.
frameworks.name: PCI Data Security Standard
frameworks.when_required: REQUIRED if handling credit card data. Card networks enforce; fines –+ per violation per month.
weaknesses: Not flexible; limited deviation from requirements allowed
Compliance does not equal security; box-ticking risk
Audit cost significant; high operational burden for compliance
strengths: Clear, prescriptive controls; easier to implement than frameworks
Industry-specific guidance for payment handling
Levels (1–4) based on transaction volume; scaled approach
Regular assessments (annual audit for Level 1) ensure continuous compliance
frameworks.primary_audience: Merchants, service providers, acquirers processing, storing credit card data

top_level_safeguards.description: Policies, workforce security, information access, workforce training, BA agreements
top_level_safeguards.name: Administrative Safeguards

top_level_safeguards.description: Facility access, workstation security, workstation use, device/media controls
top_level_safeguards.name: Physical Safeguards

top_level_safeguards.description: Access controls, audit/integrity, transmission security, encryption
top_level_safeguards.name: Technical Safeguards

frameworks.governing_body: Department of Health and Human Services (HHS)
frameworks.description: US regulation protecting PHI (patient health info). Enforced by HHS-OCR with civil/criminal penalties.
frameworks.name: HIPAA Security Rule
frameworks.when_required: MANDATORY for US healthcare providers, insurers, clearinghouses, and their business associates handling PHI
weaknesses: US-only (though may apply globally for US patient data)
Compliance can be complex for smaller providers
Penalties can be severe (– per violation, up to .5M/year per violation type)
strengths: Specific to healthcare; addresses unique PHI risks
Mandatory (not voluntary); regulatory violations have real consequences
Requires ongoing risk assessment; audit/penetration testing
Breach notification rule (notify patients within 60 days) incentivizes strong controls
frameworks.primary_audience: Covered entities (healthcare providers, payers, clearinghouses) and business associates

mappings.hipaa: Administrative Safeguards (Workforce Security), Technical Safeguards (Access Controls)
mappings.iso_27001: A.5.15 (Access Control), A.6.2 (User Access), A.8.1 (User Endpoint Devices)

mappings.pci_dss: Requirement 3 (Protect Cardholder Data), Requirement 4 (Encryption in Transit)

mappings.cis_controls: Control 7 (Email/Web Protection), Control 8 (Malware Defense), Control 12 (Vulnerability Mgmt)

mappings.hipaa: Administrative Safeguards (Incident Response), Breach Notification Rule

crosswalk.description: Mapping common control domains across frameworks to aid organizations managing multiple compliance requirements
